short: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability
intro: This chapter, The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability, covers What is Probability? Randomness and Chance, The Probability Scale from 0 to 1, Experimental Probability and Relative Frequency, Theoretical Probability: Favourable over Possible and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: What is Probability? Randomness and Chance
Probability measures how likely an event is; it matters when we know the possible outcomes but not which one will occur.
The Probability Scale from 0 to 1
Probability is measured on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); most events lie strictly between.
Experimental Probability and Relative Frequency
Experimental probability is found by doing the experiment many times: times the event occurred ÷ total trials.
Theoretical Probability: Favourable over Possible
In a fair situation with equally likely outcomes, P = number of favourable outcomes ÷ number of possible outcomes, with no experiment needed.
Probability from Statistical Data and Sampling
Survey data gives an experimental probability from a sample, which can be used to estimate counts for the whole population.
Law of Large Numbers and Gambler's Fallacy
With more trials the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability, but past results never change the next toss.
Sample Space
The sample space lists every possible outcome exactly once; its size n(S) is the total of possible outcomes.
Events as Subsets of the Sample Space
An event is any one outcome or group of outcomes of a random experiment: a subset of the sample space.
Tree Diagrams for Multi-step Experiments
A tree diagram lists all outcomes of a multi-step experiment: every path from start to end is one outcome.

items: Random experiment: can be repeated, and the result of one try cannot be predicted (coin, die). All possible results are known; which one comes up is not.
Probability P(E) measures how likely an event E is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain): 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. 0.5 means an even chance. It can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage.
Experimental probability (relative frequency) comes from data: it uses what actually happened in trials or in past records.
Law of Large Numbers: with more trials, experimental probability moves closer to the theoretical value. Small samples can be far off.
Gambler's fallacy: past results do not change the next one. A fair coin after 6 heads still gives heads with probability ½. A die after eight 4s still gives 1/6.
A sample can be used to estimate a whole group: estimate = (sample fraction) × (total).
If all outcomes are equally likely, P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (number of possible outcomes).
Equally likely: a fair coin or die, a spinner with equal parts. Not equally likely: a car starting or not, a marble from a bag with 3 red and 7 blue if we only look at colour.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E). Certain event: P = 1. Impossible event: P = 0.
Sample space S = the set of all possible outcomes. Event = a subset of S (one or more outcomes).

title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
short: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions
intro: This chapter, Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions, covers What Is a Sequence?, Explicit Rule for a Sequence, Recursive Rule for a Sequence, Arithmetic Progressions and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: What Is a Sequence?
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers; each number is a term, and the position of a term is written as a subscript, t1, t2, t3 …
Explicit Rule for a Sequence
An explicit rule uses the position n alone to calculate the nth term, so any term (53rd, 300th) is found directly.
Recursive Rule for a Sequence
A recursive rule gives the first term and then relates each term to the previous term(s); the earlier terms must be known to use it.
Arithmetic Progressions
In an arithmetic progression every term is obtained by adding the same number d to the previous term; tn = a + (n − 1)d.
Visualising an AP
Plotting (position, term) for an AP gives points on a straight line.
Sum of the First n Natural Numbers
Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: every pair adds to n + 1, so 2S = n(n + 1) and Sn = n(n + 1)/2, which is also the nth triangular number.
Geometric Progressions
In a geometric progression every term is the previous term multiplied by the same common ratio r; tn = a·r^(n−1).
Fun with Fractals
In the Sierpiński triangle the number of black triangles is 3^n (a GP with r = 3) while the black area is (3/4)^n (a GP with r = 3/4).
Visualising a GP
Points (n, tn) of a GP do not lie on a line: a GP with r > 1 climbs faster and faster, one with 0 < r < 1 falls towards 0 (bouncing ball heights).

items: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers; each number is a term: t₁, t₂, t₃, … Finite sequences end; infinite ones use "…".
Explicit rule: tₙ in terms of the position n (e.g. tₙ = 3n − 7). It gives any term directly. n must be a natural number (1, 2, 3, …).

Recursive rule: the first term(s) and a rule using earlier terms (e.g. t₁ = 1, tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + 3). Some rules use several earlier terms: Virahānka–Fibonacci 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … (each term is the sum of the previous two).
To test whether a number is a term, solve tₙ = number; it is a term only if n is a natural number.
Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, … ; square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, … (sum of the first n odd numbers).
nth term: tₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Recursive form: t₁ = a, tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d.
The points (n, tₙ) of an AP lie on a straight line.
Sum of the first n natural numbers: Sₙ = n(n + 1)/2 (write the sum forwards and backwards and add: n pairs, each n + 1). Also the nth triangular number.
Sum of consecutive numbers: m + … + k = Sₖ − Sₘ₋₁.
nth term: tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹. Recursive form: t₁ = a, tₙ = r·tₙ₋₁. Ratio r can be negative or a fraction.

title: Propositions and their Converses
intro: This chapter, Propositions and their Converses, covers Converse of a Proposition, Counterexample, Squares and an Odd Number of Factors, Divisibility Statements and Converses and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Converse of a Proposition
A proposition is a true-or-false statement; swapping its 'if' and 'then' parts gives its converse.
Counterexample
One example that contradicts a statement shows it is false; many agreeing examples never prove it.
Squares and an Odd Number of Factors
A number is a perfect square exactly when it has an odd number of factors; each direction needs its own proof.
Divisibility Statements and Converses
To test a divisibility statement, write the number as a multiple; its converse holds only when the divisors share no common factor.
Outcomes for a Proposition and Its Converse
A proposition and its converse can be true-false, true-true, false-true or false-false; each outcome has its own proof or counterexample.
Converses in Geometry
In geometry a theorem and its converse can both hold, as for Baudhayana-Pythagoras, but not always.

items: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false.
The statement "if X then Y" (also "X implies Y", or "Y when X") has the converse "if Y then X". Keep the first sentence (the setting) and swap the two parts.

A true proposition may have a false converse (it rains → the road is wet). Both can be true (equal angles ↔ equal sides in a triangle). Both can be false (n is prime → n is odd; n is odd → n is prime).
To prove a statement true, give a reason that works for every case. To show it is false, one counterexample is enough.
Always test the proposition and its converse separately; the truth of one does not tell you the other.
A counterexample is one case that makes the statement fail. Fermat's claim that 2^(2ⁿ) + 1 is always prime fails for n = 5 (Euler).
For "all numbers of the form …" claims, try n = 1, 2, 3, … until a composite number appears.
Prime p: p² has exactly 3 factors (1, p, p²); p³ has 4 factors. A product of two unequal primes has exactly 4 factors.
If n is divisible by 24, then n is divisible by 4 and by 6, but the converse is false (12). The converse holds when the two numbers share no common factor (4 and 9 give 36; 5 and 12 give 60).
Multiples: n = 6k = 3(2k), so a multiple of 6 is a multiple of 3, but 9 is a multiple of 3 and not of 6.

title: How Quantities Combine: Understanding Data
intro: This chapter, How Quantities Combine: Understanding Data, covers Average of Averages, Mixtures and Concentration, Weighted Mean and Custom Weights, Stacking Columns and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Average of Averages
The average of a whole group is the total of all its values divided by how many values there are, so each group average must be weighted by its size.
Mixtures and Concentration
The concentration of a mixture is the quantity of the ingredient divided by the quantity of the mixture, which is a mean of the concentrations.
Weighted Mean and Custom Weights
A weighted mean counts each value as many times as its weight says, so the combined result reflects how much each part matters by amount, time or.
Stacking Columns
A stacked bar chart joins the parts of each total end to end, so one picture shows the total and the parts that make it.
An Alternative to Pie Chart
A 100% stacked bar gives every total the same length, so the lengths of the parts show proportions, like a pie chart but easier to compare.
What Can We Infer?
A 100% stacked bar shows shares inside each bar, not actual numbers, so only comparisons inside one bar are safe.

items: The average of a whole group is (total of all values) ÷ (number of values). If group 1 has n values with average a, and group 2 has m values with average b, the sums are an and bm.
Combined average = (an + bm) ÷ (n + m). For three groups: (ap + bq + cr) ÷ (p + q + r).
Averaging the two averages directly gives the wrong answer when the groups have different sizes; the bigger group must count more.
If all groups have the same size, the plain average of the averages is correct.
Concentration of a mixture = (amount of the ingredient) ÷ (total amount of the mixture).
For quantities w₁, w₂, … with concentrations x₁, x₂, …: x = (w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + …) ÷ (w₁ + w₂ + …). This is the weighted mean (Brahmagupta, c. 628 CE).
Equal quantities: the answer is exactly midway. Unequal quantities: the answer is nearer the concentration with the larger quantity, and always between the smallest and largest concentrations.
Two different ingredients in one mixture: find each ingredient's amount separately and divide by the same total.
A weight shows how important (or how big) a value is. A ratio like 3 : 2 : 5 means repeat the values 3, 2 and 5 times.
Weighted mean = (w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + …) ÷ (w₁ + w₂ + …). Use it for final marks, ratings and prices of shares or gold.
A group average times its size gives its total; add totals, then divide by the total count.

title: The World of Algorithms
intro: This chapter, The World of Algorithms, covers Meaning and Parts of an Algorithm, Divisors of a Number: List and Loop, GCD by Lists of Divisors, Improving and Analysing the GCD Algorithm and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Meaning and Parts of an Algorithm
An algorithm is a systematic procedure built from basic steps that we can perform directly; it must be justified and can be analysed.
Divisors of a Number: List and Loop
To find the divisors of n, keep a list, check every j from 1 to n and add j when it divides n.
GCD by Lists of Divisors
The gcd is the rightmost entry of the list of common divisors, built from two divisor lists.
Improving and Analysing the GCD Algorithm
Refinements reduce the work but keep the answer; the work still follows the value of the smaller number.
Euclid's Subtraction Algorithm
Assuming m is at least n, gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m - n); repeat until the second number is 0.
Aryabhata's Division Algorithm
Replacing repeated subtraction by the remainder gives gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n) with effort proportional to the number of digits.

items: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, written as precisely as possible, to solve a problem. It is built from basic steps we know how to do directly (for example, adding two single digits).
An algorithm can repeat a step ("for each j in 1, 2, …, n") and can have conditional steps ("if j divides n, add j to the list").
We give names (such as j or list-of-divisors) to the values we keep track of, so that the steps can refer to them.
We must justify that an algorithm is correct, and we can analyse how many steps it takes (its efficiency).

Addition algorithm: align digits from the right, add column by column from right to left, carry 1 when a column sum is 10 or more, and write a final carry at the left. A carry is never more than 1 because 9 + 9 + 1 = 19.
Adding by counting dots needs 10 times as much work for each extra digit; the column method needs only one more column.
divisors(n): start with an empty list; for each j = 1, 2, …, n, if j divides n, add j at the end. The list comes out in increasing order.
A list (written in square brackets) is a data structure: it keeps values in order so an algorithm can use them later.
Divisors come in pairs: (1, n), (2, n/2), … so it is enough to check j up to about √n, but then the list is no longer in increasing order.
gcd (first method): find divisors(m) and divisors(n); for each x in divisors(m), if it is also in divisors(n), add it to common-divisors; the gcd is the rightmost (largest) element.
A common divisor must divide both numbers, so it cannot exceed the smaller one.
The last non-zero remainder in long division is the gcd.

title: Quadrilaterals
intro: This chapter, Quadrilaterals, covers What Exactly Is a Quadrilateral?, Properties of a Parallelogram, Tests for a Parallelogram, Midpoint Theorem and Its Converse and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: What Exactly Is a Quadrilateral?
A quadrilateral needs a careful definition: four points, no three collinear, in one plane, with the sides meeting only at the vertices.
Properties of a Parallelogram
A parallelogram has opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal and diagonals that bisect each other; each is proved with congruent triangles.
Tests for a Parallelogram
The converses of Theorem 1 are true, and each can be proved by running the original proof backwards.
Midpoint Theorem and Its Converse
The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long.
Medians and the Centroid
The three medians of a triangle pass through one point, the centroid, which divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 with the longer part at the vertex.
Midpoints of a Quadrilateral (Varignon)
The midpoints of the four sides of any quadrilateral are the vertices of a parallelogram.
Tiling the Plane Using Any 4-gon
Any quadrilateral, even an irregular or non-convex one, tiles the plane because its four angles make 360 degrees around a point.

items: A quadrilateral ABCD (4-gon) is formed by four distinct points A, B, C, D in a plane, no three on a line, joined by the sides AB, BC, CD, DA, where the sides meet only at the vertices (no crossing).
Sides AB and BC are adjacent (share a vertex); AB and CD are opposite. A and C are opposite vertices; AC and BD are the diagonals.
Convex: every internal angle is less than 180° (equivalently, the diagonals intersect). Non-convex (a dent or "dart"): one angle is more than 180°. A self-intersecting 4-gon has two sides that cross.
The angles of every (simple) quadrilateral add up to 360°, even a non-convex one.
A quadrilateral with AB ‖ DC is always convex (a trapezium).
In a parallelogram: opposite sides are equal; opposite angles are equal; diagonals bisect each other; adjacent angles add to 180°.
Proof method: run the proof backwards (the same congruence, with the tests SSS, SAS used instead of ASA).
A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle; with equal diagonals is a rectangle; with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus; with a diagonal bisecting an angle is a rhombus.
Equal diagonals alone do not make a rectangle (isosceles trapezium); add "diagonals bisect each other".
Midpoint Theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half its length.
If one vertex lies inside the triangle made by the other three, the 4-gon is non-convex.

title: Two Variables, One Line
intro: This chapter, Two Variables, One Line, covers Linear Equation in Two Variables and Its Standard Form, Solution of a Linear Equation: Ordered Pairs, The Graph of a Linear Equation: Solutions Make a Line, Understanding Slope: Rise over Run and more. Read the short notes first, check every NCERT answer, practise the important questions and then attempt the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Linear Equation in Two Variables and Its Standard Form
An equation that can be written as ax + by + c = 0 (a and b not both zero) is a linear equation in two variables; two unknowns share one relation.
Solution of a Linear Equation: Ordered Pairs
A solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that makes both sides equal; the order matters and there are infinitely many solutions.
The Graph of a Linear Equation: Solutions Make a Line
Plot the solutions and they lie on one straight line; two points fix the line, and each point on it is a solution.
Understanding Slope: Rise over Run
Slope is the steepness of a line, rise divided by run, and it is the same whichever two points of the line are used.
Slope-Intercept Form y = mx + d
In y = mx + d the number m is the slope and d is where the line crosses the y-axis; ax + by + c = 0 becomes y = mx + d when b is not 0.
A Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
Two situations about the same two unknowns give two linear equations; a solution must satisfy both at once.
Substitution Method
Express one variable in terms of the other from one equation and substitute it into the other to get one equation in one variable.
Elimination Method
Multiply so that one variable has the same coefficient in both equations, then add or subtract to eliminate it.
How Many Solutions? Unique, None or Infinitely Many
When both variables vanish in elimination the pair has none or infinitely many solutions; the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2 tell which case.
Graphical Method for a Pair of Linear Equations
Draw both lines: the meeting point is the solution; parallel lines mean no solution; coincident lines mean infinitely many.

items: A linear equation in two variables can be written in standard form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a, b are not both zero. a and b are the coefficients, c the constant.
Fractions can be cleared by multiplying by a suitable number. x = 8 is also valid: 1·x + 0·y − 8 = 0.
To frame an equation from a story, name the unknowns (x, y), write each cost or amount in terms of them, and equate to the total.
A solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that satisfies the equation. The order matters. A linear equation has infinitely many solutions.

Putting x = 0 gives the y-intercept point and y = 0 gives the x-axis point: two points are enough to draw the graph, which is a straight line. Every point of the line is a solution, and every solution is a point of the line.
If c = 0 the line passes through the origin. Multiplying or dividing an equation by a non-zero number gives an equation with the same solutions.
Slope = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁) for any two points of a line; it is the same for any pair of points and either order.
Positive slope: rising to the right. Negative slope: falling. Zero slope: horizontal line (y = k).
y = mx + d: m is the slope, d is the y-intercept (the line cuts the y-axis at (0, d)). From ax + by + c = 0 (b ≠ 0): m = −a/b and d = −c/b.
Steeper means larger rise ÷ run (compare the ratios as decimals).
To check a point, substitute it. If LHS = RHS, the point is on the line.
To compare steepness, divide rise by run for each and compare the numbers.

topics: Cuboids and Cubes
A cuboid is a 3D version of a rectangle: its surface is six rectangles (TSA = 2(wl + hl + hw)) and its volume is the number of unit cubes inside (V =.
Right Circular Cylinder
Cutting a right circular cylinder open gives a rectangle, so CSA = circumference x height = 2 pi r h.
Cones
A cone unrolls into a sector, so CSA = pi r l; its volume is exactly one third of the cylinder on the same base and height.
Pyramidal Shapes
A pyramid joins every point of a base to one apex; its volume is 1/3 x base area x height for any base, and its surface area is the sum of its faces.
Spheres and Hemispheres
A sphere's surface area equals the curved surface of the tight cylinder around it (4 pi r2) and its volume is 1/3 x surface area x radius = 4/3 pi.
Areas and Volumes Around Us
A guesstimate is a reasoned estimate when exact data are missing: guess first, model the quantities, assume sensibly, calculate with approximations.

items: Cuboid: 6 rectangular faces, edges l, w, h. TSA = 2(lw + wh + hl). Volume V = lwh = area of base × height.
Cube of side a: TSA = 6a², V = a³. (Special case of the cuboid with l = w = h.)
Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³). 1 m³ = 10,00,000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³; 1 ft³ ≈ 28.3 litres.
Same volume does not mean same surface area: a cube needs the least covering for a given volume.
Cutting a solid into pieces keeps the volume the same but increases the total surface area.
A right circular cylinder has a circular cross-section and its axis is perpendicular to the base.
Cut open, the curved surface is a rectangle: circumference × height. CSA = 2πrh.
Closed at both ends: TSA = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r). Open at one end (a tumbler): 2πrh + πr².
V = πr²h (area of cross-section × height).
If the radius is doubled, the volume becomes 4 times; if the height is doubled, the volume becomes 2 times.
Number of small boxes in a big one = volume of big ÷ volume of small (if they fit exactly).
Ratio questions: write each measure as a product (for example r²h) and divide; the π cancels.
First find l from l² = h² + r². Slant height is for area, vertical height is for volume.
